Hi Stacey=2C
Sounds like a neat study. =20


The key assumption is that every point in your buffered area needs to have =
equal probability of being sampled if you want your mean density of plants =
to have any meaning. You don't have to orient your transects randomly alon=
g the trail or road=2C but I think you still need some randomisation. From=
the comfort of my home=2C it's easy for me to say that the best approach w=
ould be to orient all transects perpendicular to the road/trail=2C and then=
place them systematically with a random start point. If a small fraction =
of these transects can't be surveyed because of steep topography=2C that's =
fine=2C as long as it's negligible=2C or that you can exclude that kind of =
habitat from the survey region across which you estimate abundance. If the=
y can't be surveyed because of thick vegetation=2C that's a problem=2C beca=
use that's no doubt confounded with your parameter of interest (density of =
vegetation). If this turns out to be a very labour-intensive task=2C I'd f=
ocus on doing fewer transects well (but still aiming for at least 20 in eac=
h stratum)=2C rather than collecting hundreds of transects that are biased =
because you missed the habitat of interest. =20


We ran into similar problems in a survey for marine mammals in a complex fj=
ord habitat. I gave Len Thomas the best digital map I had of our survey ar=
ea. It turned out not to be very good=2C and when we did the survey=2C som=
e fraction of the transects (~1%=2C I think) turned out to be in waters too=
shallow to navigate. Len wrote up the design as a methods paper=2C which =
is found here:
http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/len/papers/ThomasJCRM2007.pdf


and our results are found here:
http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/len/papers/WilliamsJCRM2007.pdf


Len wrote some practical advice about what to do in situations like this. =
I hope these papers are of some help to you. =20


Best=2C
Rob

messages.author: 6e15de0134e98c08
messages.subject: Re: distance sampling to estimate density of invasive plants
parts:
Hi Stacey, list,

I must disagree with Rob's initial statement, even if I agree with most=20
of his other comments. The key assumption here is that the distribution=20
of animals within the strips is uniform for conventional methods to work.

You got me confused with your quote to Buckland et al. 2009, but then a=20
google search showed me that you were actually referring to the 2001=20
book. Having said that, in my opinion, the case mentioned there does not=20
really apply in your context. What you have is a density gradient of the=20
objects of interest, something which could produce very large bias (see=20
e.g. Marques et al 2010. Point transect sampling along linear features.=20
Biometrics, for an example with over 100% bias). This happens because=20
conventional methods assume that the distribution of animals within the=20
search strips is uniform, something which is plausible under random line=20
placement, but which we know is not true under you scenario.

If the buffer around the road you are interested in is small compared to=20
the distances at which you can detect plants, then using a MRDS approach=20
(e.g. Borchers et al 2006) or even a MR (with distance as a covariate=20
approach?), see e.g.

Fletcher, J. R. & Hutto, L. R. Estimating detection probabilities of=20
river birds using double surveys The Auk, 2006, 123, 695-707

might be enough, but if that is not the case, I can't see how to solve=20
your problem without leaving the roads.

Rob's suggestion of transects perpendicular to the road, systematic with=20
a random start, could work, as that presumably would "cut" across the=20
density gradient, so conventional methods might work.

If you can't do that, another approach might be to have some=20
perpendicular lines to estimate the density gradient, plus some lines=20
along the roads. The right likelihood would allow you to estimate=20
density under such scenario, but that's not in a paper yet, but see=20
chapters 4 and 5 in my PhD thesis

Marques, T. A. Incorporating measurement error and density gradients in=20
distance sampling surveys University of St Andrews, 2007

Under your setting, it seems like a spatial model based approach might=20
also be useful, as density might be well predicted as a function of some=20
covariates, namely, distance from road/trail.

Hope this helps

T.
